"Puny" describes something — or someone — that is both small and weak, to the point of being noticeably inadequate or unimpressive. The key thing to understand right away is that "puny" is almost never just about size alone, and rarely just about weakness alone. It is the combination of both, wrapped in a sense that the thing falls far short of what is expected or needed. If you call something puny, you are essentially saying: this is disappointingly little, and it shows.
The Emotional Tone: There Is Always a Judgment in It

This is perhaps the most important thing to understand about "puny" — it is almost never a neutral word. It carries a strong tone of contempt, dismissiveness, or quiet mockery. When someone describes a person, an effort, or an amount as puny, there is an implied sneer behind it, as though the speaker is saying, "Is that really all?" or "How laughably small."

Even when there is no deliberate cruelty intended, the word still signals that the speaker views the subject as clearly below the expected standard. This emotional color is what makes "puny" feel much stronger and more loaded than a plain word like "small" or "weak."
When Used to Describe a Person or Living Creature

When "puny" describes a person or animal, it refers to their physical build — they are unusually small, thin, and visibly lacking in physical strength. It paints a picture of a body that looks like it could not handle much of a physical challenge.

For example: "The other kids on the team were tall and strong, but Marcus was a puny child who struggled to carry his own backpack."

Or: "The lion cub was puny next to its massive, powerful mother."

It is worth noting that calling a person "puny" is almost always unkind. They would very likely feel insulted. You should be careful about using it to describe real people to their faces.

"Puny" is not limited to bodies and sizes. It is widely and commonly used for abstract things — efforts, excuses, amounts of money, results, or anything that feels insufficient given the situation.

For example: "He offered a puny apology that convinced absolutely no one." Here, the apology was weak and inadequate — far too small for what the situation called for.

Or: "The government donated a puny sum to help the flood victims." The amount was embarrassingly small given the scale of the disaster.

Or: "Her puny excuse didn't hold up for even a second." The excuse was feeble and unconvincing.

In all these cases, the word carries that same core message: the thing is not enough, and it shows.

"Puny" is very often used in comparison — something is puny relative to something else that is bigger, stronger, or more impressive. The contrast between the two things is what gives the word its punch.

For example: "Our little fishing boat looked absolutely puny next to the enormous cargo ship."

Or: "Standing next to the professional athletes, the rookie felt puny and out of place."

This comparative quality also means "puny" is sometimes used to express awe at something large and powerful, by showing how small everything else seems beside it. If a character in a story says, "These puny humans cannot stop me!" — they are not just insulting humans; they are also communicating their own great power by contrast.

Understanding the words closest to "puny" in meaning will sharpen your sense of exactly what makes it unique.

Feeble focuses more on weakness than on small size — a feeble person may not necessarily be small, but they lack strength. Frail suggests delicacy and the risk of being easily broken, with less emphasis on inadequacy. Scrawny focuses on thin, bony physical appearance and is almost exclusively about the body. Meager and paltry are used for amounts and quantities — a meager salary, a paltry reward — and are more neutral in tone than "puny." Undersized is the most neutral of all: it simply states that something is smaller than the standard, without the contempt.

"Puny" is the most expressive of all these in terms of contempt, and it is the clearest in combining both smallness and weakness in one single word. It also has a slight theatrical, almost dramatic quality that the others lack, which is why villains in films and stories are so fond of using it.

The opposite of puny would be words like: mighty, powerful, robust, formidable, substantial, impressive.

Many learners assume "puny" simply means "small." This is incomplete and can lead you to use it wrongly.

Something can be small without being puny. A small but flawlessly cut diamond is not puny. A small but ferocious warrior is not puny. A short but extraordinarily powerful gymnast is not puny.

The essential ingredient that "puny" always carries is the sense that the smallness or weakness makes the thing inadequate, pathetic, or laughably below expectation. Without that judgment of insufficiency baked in, you are probably looking for a different word.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Think of "puny" as a word that carries a picture and a feeling at once. The picture is of something visibly small and frail. The feeling is a slight curl of the lip — a dismissive, unimpressed reaction. Whether the word is describing a thin child, a weak excuse, a tiny salary, or a feeble effort, it always communicates the same thing: this is small, weak, and not enough — and anybody can see that.
